blocks.text: “Mighty Miniatures” Features Over 300 Tiny Artworks From Indigenous Communities Across the Western Hemisphere
Opening November 21 at the National Museum of the American Indian in New York, this exhibition includes masterpieces created over a span of nearly two centuries.

blocks.alt: “Mighty Miniatures” Features Over 300 Tiny Artworks From Indigenous Communities Across the Western Hemisphere

blocks.text: “ Mighty Miniatures ,” an exhibition celebrating the intricate art of miniatures, is on view at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian in New York from Saturday, November 21 through Friday, August 20, 2027. Curated by Anya Montiel (Tohono O’odham descent), the exhibition features over 300 pieces of art that showcase the skill of Indigenous weavers, sculptors, carvers and other artists that work on a miniscule scale.

The exhibition includes tiny masterpieces created over a span of nearly two centuries by artists from Indigenous communities from North and South America, as well as Hawai'i and the Caribbean. The small works reflect worldviews and cultural expressions, encouraging play and transferring intergenerational knowledge.

“‘Mighty Miniatures’ brings together some of the smallest works in the museum collection, reaching across the Western Hemisphere and spanning nearly 200 years,” Montiel said. “It is amazing to see how these miniatures have been made with such skill, ingenuity, and detail. This exhibition is a celebration of Indigenous artistry on a small scale and the artists who create them.”
Left: Nahua doll’s chair, no date. Wood, yarn. 0.7 x 0.5 in. (14/4064); right: Tohono O’odham I’itoi ki: (Man-in-the-Maze) miniature basket, ca. 2000. Arizona. Horsehair. 4 x 2.6 in. 26/8865
The exhibition is divided into six sections:
Playing with Scale introduces visitors to the concept of miniatures, placing small works alongside their full-sized equivalents.

Play Is Important! highlights miniatures as essential teaching tools for children to learn about their world and practice adult skills, and includes cradleboards, mother and child figures, dolls, and clothing.
Watercraft shows Indigenous models of canoes, kayaks, and other vessels designed to navigate rivers, lakes, and oceans across the Americas.

Architecture reflects a diversity of Indigenous housing styles and materials to refute the stereotype that “all Indians live in tipis” with examples from the Northern Cheyenne, Navajo, Zuni, Yupik, Iñupiaq, and Kichwa peoples.
Skill and Artistry explains one of the reasons why Indigenous artists make miniatures. It is a way for artists to showcase their mastery of materials and techniques.

Tourism and the Art Market features some miniatures that have become collectible works of art, like Alaskan ivory carvings and Maine fancy baskets, with people seeking miniatures for their personal collections.

Left: Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) canoe model, no date. Minnesota, Birchbark, sinew, paint. 0.5 x 2.4 x 1.1 in. (20/4941); right: Floyd Kingeekuk Sr. (Siberian Yupik, 1933–2006), ringed seal figure, 1975. Savoonga, Alaska. Ivory, ink. 0.9 x 4.1 x 1.2 in. (27/684)

A family-friendly opening program is scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 12, 11 AM–4 PM. Multi-disciplinary artist Lance Cardinal (Cree), a finalist on the TV show Best In Miniature , will lead visitors in mini drum making sessions. Gallery tours by Montiel will illuminate the stories behind the objects and discuss how the exhibition came together.
Plan your visit and get tickets at AmericanIndian.si.edu .
